title: How a sprout knows up from down
description: Bury a seed any way up and the sprout still gets it right: roots dive down, shoots climb up. The seed carries its own sense of gravity, built from tiny falling grains inside its cells.

body.heading: Tiny stones that settle
paragraphs: Inside certain plant cells are dense grains called statoliths — heavier than the fluid around them, so they settle to whichever side of the cell faces down, like pebbles sinking in a jar of water. Their settling tells the plant which way is down. This response to gravity is called gravitropism.

Roots grow toward gravity (positive gravitropism) and shoots grow against it (negative gravitropism), steered by the same growth chemical, auxin, that bends shoots toward light — distributed unevenly according to the statoliths' report.

body.heading: Why it cannot be fooled for long
paragraphs: Lay a seedling on its side and within hours the shoot tip curves upward and the root tip downward, each re-aiming itself. Astronauts growing plants in orbit, where nothing settles, have watched roots wander without gravity's instructions — proof of how much the seed relies on falling grains.
For the seed, the system is life insurance: buried at any angle, in darkness, it can still send its first root to water and its first shoot to light.

takeaway: A sprout finds up and down using statoliths — dense grains that settle inside its cells — steering roots down toward water and shoots up toward light.
